title: Build a feedback theme tracker
description: A system that pulls in tickets, reviews, and surveys, and returns them clustered into ranked themes backed by quotes.

api.title: API (Application Programming Interface)
api.content: A way for two programs to talk to each other. When a tool says 'connect via API,' it means software can send requests and get data back automatically — no manual copy-paste needed.

agent.title: Agent
agent.content: An AI that works independently to complete a goal — planning steps, picking tools, running them, and deciding what to do next without you prompting it at every step. Unlike a chatbot, an agent takes action.

model.title: Model
model.content: A specific trained version of an AI. Claude has several models (like Opus, Sonnet, Haiku) that differ in capability and speed. Larger models are smarter but slower; smaller ones are faster and cheaper.

skill.title: Skill
skill.content: A plain-text file with instructions for a specific repeatable workflow. Save it once, then trigger it with a slash command like /research-competitive. Same steps and output format every time — like a macro for Claude.

claude.title: Claude
claude.content: The AI made by Anthropic. Available as a chat tool at claude.ai, as a desktop app (Claude Desktop), and as a terminal tool (Claude Code). The different interfaces are suited for different types of work.

prompt.title: Prompt
prompt.content: The instruction or message you give to an AI. The quality of your prompt directly shapes the quality of the output. Writing better prompts is one of the highest-leverage skills in this program.

rubric.title: Rubric
rubric.content: The written definition of what a good output looks like, in 3–5 scoreable dimensions. Evals grade against a rubric; without one, 'is this good?' is a vibe, not a measurement.

chatgpt.title: ChatGPT
chatgpt.content: OpenAI's chat assistant. The most widely known AI tool — works similarly to Claude but with different strengths and weaknesses. Useful to have access to for cross-checking outputs or trying alternate models.

workflow.title: Workflow
workflow.content: A multi-step process Claude runs to accomplish a goal — for example: read emails → filter by topic → summarize → post to Slack. Workflows can be run manually or on a schedule.

read-only.title: Read-only
read-only.content: The first rung of the trust gradient: the agent can see your inbox, calendar, or docs but can't change anything. The default starting state for every new tool connection. Tiny blast radius, fast to ship, and confirms the read side works before you graduate the write side.

tool-connectors.title: Tool Connectors
tool-connectors.content: Integrations that let Claude read from and write to apps you use (Gmail, Slack, Google Calendar, Notion, HubSpot, etc.). Set up once in Customize → Connectors. Each connector opens up a new category of tasks Claude can automate.

children.text: Product leaders now name synthesizing customer signals a top-three time drain, up 68% from 41% three years ago, and most teams watch feedback scattered across 7 to 9 separate channels at once, per [Perspective AI's buyer's guide to feedback tools](https://getperspective.ai/blog/ai-product-feedback-tools-in-2026-a-buyer-s-guide-for-product-teams). This system reads tickets, reviews, and survey responses, clusters them into themes ranked by frequency and severity, and returns each theme with the quotes that back it up, linked to source.

[OpenAI's own product playbook](https://academy.openai.com/public/clubs/work-users-ynjqu/resources/use-cases-product) names this build directly, calling out the most frequent themes in a feedback set with example quotes, then converting the pain points into a feature-idea shortlist.

Run it as a weekly paste-in [prompt](#tooltip-prompt), a saved [skill](#tooltip-skill), or a scheduled [agent](#tooltip-agent) that pulls from your support tool and survey exports and posts a ranked digest to a shared doc or chat. Every version stays [read-only](#tooltip-read-only) against your feedback sources.

Open your AI chat and have it interview you into a scope document. Done means a written scope naming your feedback sources, your ranking rules, what a representative quote needs, and how often it runs.

children.prompt: I want to build a system with my AI tool that clusters customer feedback into themes I can act on. Ask me questions, one at a time, about which feedback sources to pull in, how often to run it, whether frequency or severity matters more for ranking, and what a representative quote needs to include. When you have what you need, write it up as a scope document I can build from.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: the interview surfaces decisions you didn't know you needed to make, and the scope document becomes the brief for every build session after it.

items: Which support tool, survey tool, and review source feed the clustering, and how to export each cleanly.
Whether frequency or severity drives the ranking when the two disagree.
What a representative quote needs to include so it stays traceable back to source.

children.text: Bring the scope document. Pressure-test it first by pasting it into a fresh session or a different [model](#tooltip-model) and asking it to poke holes. Then gather any access it calls for. Common connectors are your support tool (Zendesk and Intercom publish official connectors and [API](#tooltip-api) docs), a survey tool for intake, and a sheet or doc for the running history. The paste-in version needs none.
**Create.** Build and test the system on a real export, every source included for the period. The prompt below is one example; your scope document has the full version.

children.prompt:
Goal: Cluster my raw customer feedback into ranked, evidence-backed themes.

Context: [Paste your export of tickets, reviews, and survey responses for the period. Note the product areas you want it to watch.]

Rules:
- Return no more than 8 themes.
- Rank by frequency and severity, stated separately.
- Attach 2-3 representative quotes per theme, each with a source link.
- Never merge two distinct complaints into one theme because the wording overlaps.
- Flag any single high-severity report on its own, even if it only appears once.
- Output as a ranked list: theme name, frequency, severity, quotes with source.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: separating frequency from severity and forcing a source link on every quote keeps a loud minority complaint from reading as consensus.

children.text: **Review.** Check the output against your scope. Themes distinct, quotes traceable, the lone high-severity report still surfaced?
**Feedback.** Tell it exactly what went wrong ("those two are different complaints, split them") and fold each correction into the rules.

items: Schedule it. Connect your support and survey tools through a [tool connector](#tooltip-tool-connectors) and have the digest arrive weekly.
Track how each theme trends week over week instead of a single snapshot.
Route new high-severity, low-frequency reports straight to chat the moment they land.

children.text: **Measure** with a [rubric](#tooltip-rubric). Have your AI chat draft the rubric and a run log in one pass.

children.prompt: From my scope document, write a rubric for judging each theme cluster, with 4 to 6 pass/fail checks. Then set up a simple run log I can keep in a doc or spreadsheet, with columns for date, themes returned, themes that held up on review, complaints wrongly merged, high-severity reports missed, and what rule I changed. Give me both in a format I can paste into my notes.
children.prompt_note: How this prompt works: pass/fail checks remove the judgment call, and the log columns make recurring misfires visible after a few runs.

children.text: **Log** every run against the rubric. Note the date, which checks passed or failed, and what changed. A single miss is noise, and a repeated miss is an instruction you haven't written yet.

**Make skills** from what the log shows. Once the rubric passes a few runs straight, package the prompt and your corrected rules into a reusable AI skill, so every run starts from your defaults. A repeated failure earns its own skill. [Claude](#tooltip-claude)'s built-in skill-creator skill will interview you and write it, and a custom GPT does the same in [ChatGPT](#tooltip-chatgpt).

One durable failure mode. Clustering can quietly merge two different complaints that share vocabulary into one theme, so check on every run that quotes still trace back to source and no two distinct issues got flattened into one.
